blocks.text: Between 2000-2050 the proportion of the world's population over 60 will double from ~==11%== to ~==22%==, with the absolute number rising from **605 million to 2 billion**. In the **UK**, 10 million people are over 65 (one sixth of the population), projected to reach 19 million (one quarter) by 2050; 3 million are over 80. Average spending for retired households is **nearly double** that of non-retired households.

The National Service Framework for Older People (2001), Everybody's Business (2005) and No Health Without Mental Health (2011) established that older people's mental health needs input from both health and social care and that services should be age-appropriate and non-discriminatory. Reducing specialist older-adult services in favour of "ageless" services has been flagged as potentially breaching the Equality Act 2010 via indirect discrimination.

blocks.title: RCPsych Needs-Based Criteria for Older People's Mental Health Services
rows: People of any age with a primary dementia
People with mental disorder **and** physical illness/frailty that contributes to or complicates management of their mental illness (may include people under 65)

People with psychological/social difficulties related to the ageing process or end-of-life issues, or who feel their needs may be best met by an older people's service — **this would normally include people over the age of 70**

blocks.text: **JCPMH** commissioning guidance key points: services must be commissioned on the basis of need, not age alone; must address functional illness (depression, psychosis) as well as dementia; older people should have access to community crisis/home treatment services and dedicated liaison services in acute hospitals; they respond well to psychological input.

==30%== of carers of people with mental health problems will suffer depression at some stage; inability of a carer to continue providing support is a recognised trigger for a move from home into long-term care.

Specialist assessment domains: cognitive, functional, physical health (and its interaction with mental health), carer needs, and capacity (Mental Capacity Act, Deprivation of Liberty Safeguards). Home assessment has particular advantages for people with dementia — depth/quality of information and avoiding a tiring, expensive journey.

bullets.text: **NSF for Older People** (2001), **Everybody's Business** (2005) and **No Health Without Mental Health** (2011) require age-appropriate, non-discriminatory services — replacing specialist older-adult services with "ageless" services risks indirect discrimination under the **Equality Act 2010**.
**JCPMH** commissioning: services must be need-based (not age alone), cover functional illness as well as dementia, and give access to community crisis/home treatment and acute liaison services.
A carer's inability to continue support is a recognised trigger for a move into long-term care; home assessment gives richer information for dementia patients and avoids a tiring, costly journey.

blocks.text: In Parkinson's disease, depression occurs in ~2/3 of patients and dementia in ~==40%==; common cognitive deficits are executive dysfunction, attention, memory, visuomotor processing and visual attention. Medication timing matters — missed doses can cause delirium, depression, slowed cognition and anxiety.
Delirium affects 30-==40%== of people in the week after a stroke. Pathological crying/emotional lability is common post-stroke and can be treated with SSRIs.

Charles Bonnet syndrome (visual hallucinations without psychotic symptoms) is most commonly associated with macular degeneration, also cataracts and diabetic retinopathy. Auditory impairment has been associated with psychotic symptoms in the elderly.

**Emotional reaction to illness**: reaction to physical illness depends on premorbid personality, perceived threat of the illness, treatment required and treatment experience. Anxious individuals may develop pathological anxiety due to an increased focus on and morbid interpretation of physical sensations. **Metabolic changes** during illness — dehydration, electrolyte imbalance, endocrine changes and infection — can all accentuate or produce affective symptoms. Adjustment disorders are common following physical illness and, by their nature, are transient.

Depression is ~2-3x more common with a chronic physical health problem, occurring in ~==20%== of the chronically physically ill. **NICE**: no evidence supports a specific antidepressant choice per physical illness — a generic **SSRI** should be first line; note SSRIs may worsen hyponatraemia or increase bleeding risk.

bullets.text: In **PD**, missed medication doses can themselves cause delirium, depression, slowed cognition and anxiety — not just under-treatment of motor symptoms.
Post-stroke pathological crying/emotional lability is common and treatable with **SSRIs**.

Charles Bonnet syndrome (visual hallucinations, no other psychosis) is linked most to macular degeneration, also cataracts/diabetic retinopathy; auditory impairment is linked to psychotic symptoms in the elderly.
**NICE**: no antidepressant is specifically better for a given physical illness — a generic **SSRI** is first-line, but watch for hyponatraemia and increased bleeding risk.

rows: Normal pressure hydrocephalus; subdural haematoma; cerebral tumours; general paralysis of the insane
Alcoholism; anoxia; hypoglycaemia; myxoedema; vitamin deficiencies; drug/chemical poisoning; pseudodementia; renal/hepatic disease

blocks.text: Alcohol-related dementia accounts for ==12%== of young-onset dementia cases; memory impairment may be static and can improve with abstinence; autobiographical memory is often affected and confabulation can occur.

Normal pressure hydrocephalus: triad of dementia, gait ataxia and urinary incontinence, with gait disturbance always preceding other symptoms; population prevalence ==0.4%== (Trenkwalder et al 1995); ==50%== idiopathic, ==50%== secondary to mechanical **CSF** obstruction. **CSF** tap test (40-50ml withdrawn) has low sensitivity/negative predictive value. **VP** shunt candidates are best selected when **NPH** is secondary to an identified cause, and gait is the feature most likely to improve; milder dementia predicts better outcome.

Chronic subdural haematoma: bilateral in ==30%== of cases; a history of head injury is present in only ==50%==; the clot can be isodense (and thus missed) on **CT** during the first 3 weeks. Mortality is ~==10%==, highest with depressed consciousness and bilateral haematomas.

bullets.text: Alcohol-related dementia memory impairment can be static and improve with abstinence; autobiographical memory affected, confabulation may occur.

**NPH** triad (dementia, gait ataxia, urinary incontinence) — gait disturbance always comes first; ==50%== idiopathic/==50%== secondary; **CSF** tap test has poor sensitivity; gait is most likely to improve after **VP** shunt, and milder dementia predicts a better outcome.
Subdural haematoma: head-injury history present in only ==50%==; clot can be isodense (missed) on **CT** in the first 3 weeks; mortality highest with depressed consciousness and bilateral clots.

blocks.text: Huntington's disease dementia: autosomal dominant **CAG** repeat expansion on the Huntingtin gene; presents typically in the 4th decade with frontal dementia and movement disorder; recall is affected more than recognition, suggesting a retrieval rather than encoding problem.

Multiple sclerosis dementia: **MRI** is the key diagnostic test, though distinguishing demyelination from vascular damage can be difficult in older adults; **CSF** examination and evoked potentials can confirm diagnosis. Other secondary causes include **HIV** dementia, Wilson's disease and limbic encephalitis.

Sporadic **CJD**: caused by the protease-resistant prion protein PrPSc; ==85%== spontaneous/sporadic, ==10%== genetic mutation, ==5%== iatrogenic (dural/corneal graft, pituitary growth hormone). **EEG** shows 'periodic complexes' (less frequent in genetic/growth-hormone-related cases, never seen in variant **CJD**). **CSF** 14-3-3 protein is often elevated but is non-specific. Definitive diagnosis requires post-mortem spongiform degeneration sparing white matter tracts. Treatment is symptomatic — sodium **valproate** and **clonazepam** may reduce movement disorder severity.

Variant **CJD** followed the **BSE** epidemic; affects mainly young men in their 20s; early anxiety/depressive symptoms progress to personality change then dementia, with prominent ataxia and myoclonus over a 1-2 year course. The pulvinar sign (symmetric high signal in the pulvinar/medial thalamus on **FLAIR** **MRI**) is diagnostic, seen in >==70%== of confirmed cases. Tonsillar biopsy for prion immunostaining is sensitive and specific.

Linked to **BSE**; young adults (20s); early anxiety/depression then personality change then dementia; pulvinar sign on **MRI**; **EEG** shows no distinctive periodic changes
Presentation similar to **CJD** but longer course to death (up to ~5 years)
Rare inherited prion disease (not separately detailed in this source beyond being one of the four human prion diseases)

sections.title: 5. Alzheimer's Disease — Epidemiology, Genetics & Risk Factors

blocks.text: **AD** is the most common dementia; onset usually 40-90, most often after 65. Risk is ==1%== at age 60, doubling every 5 years, reaching ==40%== by age 85. Beyond age 75, **AD** risk is six times that of vascular dementia. Age at onset is earlier with a family history. Final diagnosis technically requires neuropathological examination.

blocks.title: Alzheimer's Disease — Risk Factors
rows: Age; Down's syndrome; apolipoprotein ε4 allele
Female sex; head injury; postmenopausal oestrogen decline
Family history of Down's syndrome; family history of Parkinson's disease; vascular factors

blocks.text: Genetics: Presenilin 2 (chromosome 1) and Presenilin 1 (chromosome 14) cause early-onset disease; the amyloid precursor protein (**APP**) gene is on the long arm of chromosome 21 (explaining the near-universal early **AD** pathology in trisomy 21/Down's syndrome, and a mutation at codon 717 also causes excess amyloid deposition). Apolipoprotein ε4 (chromosome 19) increases late-onset **AD** risk — one ε4 copy gives 3x the incidence, two copies gives 8x — but genetic testing for ε4 is not recommended clinically since it occurs in people without dementia and not in all **AD** cases.

blocks.title: Chromosomal loci implicated in Alzheimer's disease genetics
rows: Early-onset **AD**; extra copy in Down's syndrome (trisomy 21)
Increases risk of late-onset **AD** (3x with 1 copy, 8x with 2 copies)

blocks.text: Probable **AD** requires dementia established clinically/neuropsychologically, deficits in ≥2 cognitive domains, progressive worsening, no disturbance of consciousness, and absence of another systemic/brain disease that could explain the deficits.

**NINCDS-ADRDA** probable-**AD** criteria trap: cerebral atrophy on **CT** is **NOT** a required criterion (it only helps exclude other causes) — a frequently tested "which is **NOT** required" question.

Psychiatric: delusions in ==15%==, hallucinations (auditory/visual) in 10-==15%==, depression requiring treatment in ==20%==. Average survival is ~8 years.

blocks.text: Psychosis occurs in 30-==50%== of **AD**; delusions are more common than hallucinations (Bassiony et al 2000); visual and auditory hallucinations are both common (Tariot 1995); psychosis is associated with more rapid cognitive decline (Forstl et al 1994).

bullets.text: Cognitive symptoms: short-term memory deficit progressing to long-term (amnesia mainly for recent events), disorientation especially for time, expressive/receptive dysphasia and anomia, apraxia, agnosia, and impaired visuospatial/executive function.

Probable **AD** needs dementia established clinically/neuropsychologically, deficits in ≥2 cognitive domains, progressive worsening, no impaired consciousness, and no other explanatory disease — cerebral atrophy on **CT** is **NOT** a required criterion, only supportive.

Misidentification delusions (Capgras, phantom boarder, mirror sign, **TV** sign, magazine sign) are a recognised **AD** psychosis cluster (Karim & Burns 2003); psychosis overall is linked to more rapid cognitive decline.

blocks.text: **Donepezil**, **rivastigmine** and **galantamine** are cholinesterase inhibitors licensed for mild-moderate **AD**. **Donepezil** has a long half-life (70 hours, once-daily dosing), near-total plasma protein binding, and mainly **GI** side effects (nausea, vomiting, diarrhoea, anorexia; also headache, dizziness, syncope, muscle cramps). **Rivastigmine** and **galantamine** cause more **GI** and neuropsychiatric adverse effects than **donepezil**.

**Galantamine** has a direct nicotinic stimulatory action. **Rivastigmine** inhibits both acetylcholinesterase and butyrylcholinesterase, is available as a once-daily transdermal patch, and improves both cognition and ADLs in Parkinson's disease dementia.

blocks.title: Antidementia drug mechanisms of action
rows: Reversible, non-competitive inhibitor of both acetylcholinesterase and butyrylcholinesterase
Reversible, competitive acetylcholinesterase inhibitor; also a nicotinic receptor allosteric modulator/agonist
Non-competitive **NMDA** receptor antagonist (also weak 5-**HT3** antagonist); affects glutamate transmission

blocks.title: Antidementia drug starting and treatment doses

blocks.text: **Memantine** is a non-competitive, **PCP**-site **NMDA** antagonist, theoretically neuroprotective against glutamate excitotoxicity and thus termed disease-modifying; better tolerated than cholinesterase inhibitors (main side effects dizziness, headache, fatigue, diarrhoea, gastric pain). Used in moderate-severe **AD**, or mild-moderate **AD** when cholinesterase inhibitors are not tolerated/contraindicated (e.g. severe cardiac conduction defects or severe asthma).

**CSM** review (Duff 2004): **olanzapine** and **risperidone** were each associated with at least a two-fold increase in stroke risk and should no longer be used in dementia — but Herrmann et al (2004) found no difference in stroke risk between **olanzapine**/**risperidone** and typical neuroleptics in dementia treatment.

The Duff (2004) **CSM** restriction (**olanzapine**/**risperidone** associated with a 2x stroke risk increase in dementia) is deliberately contrasted with Herrmann et al (2004), who found **NO** significant difference in stroke risk vs typical neuroleptics — both study findings are independently examinable, and the exam expects you to know the regulatory position (Duff/**CSM**) governs practice regardless of the conflicting evidence (Herrmann).

Antidementia drug choice by comorbidity is examined as a matching exercise, not a single "best drug" fact: **rivastigmine** transdermal patch avoids **GI** side effects for a patient benefiting from but intolerant of oral **rivastigmine**; **rivastigmine** (not **donepezil**) is favoured in cardiovascular disease owing to minimal interaction potential; **donepezil** is favoured when avoiding **GI**/neuropsychiatric effects generally.

bullets.text: **Donepezil**: long half-life (70h, once daily), near-total protein binding, mainly **GI** side effects. **Rivastigmine**/**galantamine** cause more **GI**/neuropsychiatric effects than **donepezil**.

**Galantamine** has a direct nicotinic stimulatory action; **rivastigmine** inhibits both acetyl- and butyryl-cholinesterase, comes as a once-daily patch, and helps cognition/**ADLs** in **PD** dementia.

**Memantine** (**NMDA** antagonist) is better tolerated than cholinesterase inhibitors; used in moderate-severe **AD**, or mild-moderate **AD** if cholinesterase inhibitors aren't tolerated (e.g. severe cardiac conduction defects/asthma).
**CSM** (Duff 2004): **olanzapine**/**risperidone** each carry ≥2x stroke risk in dementia and should not be used — though Herrmann et al (2004) found no difference vs typical neuroleptics.
Ginkgo biloba's benefit on cognition is unconvincing (Cochrane 2007); tacrine is rarely used owing to hepatotoxicity.

blocks.text: Vascular dementia is the second most common cause of dementia (==20%== of cases). **NINCDS-AIREN** criteria require cerebrovascular disease on exam and imaging plus a temporal relationship: dementia within 3 months of a stroke, **OR** abrupt deterioration/fluctuating stepwise course. A median of 4.5 neurological signs per patient is seen; reflex asymmetry is the most prevalent sign (==49%==).

**Hachinski score discrepancy**: the source book marks only Abrupt onset, Fluctuating course, Focal neurological symptoms and Focal neurological signs with "(2)" and states "unless marked, each item scores one point" — by that literal wording, **History of strokes scores 1**, not the 2 shown in the table above (which follows the standard, widely-published Hachinski Ischaemic Score that does weight prior stroke at 2). A question drawn directly from this book's wording could expect 1 point; one drawn from the general scale could expect 2 — know both.

Three clinical subtypes: cognitive deficits after a single stroke (more often midbrain/thalamic, may remain fixed or recover); multi-infarct dementia (stepwise deterioration, minor ischaemic episodes, periods of stability); progressive small vessel disease/Binswanger's disease (subcortical dementia, slow decline, generalised slowing, gait disturbance/dysarthria; **MRI** shows lacunae or leukoaraiosis).

Risk factors: old age, hypertension (positive history in ==50%==), ischaemic heart disease, smoking, alcohol, hyperlipidaemia, atrial fibrillation, family history, valvular disease, atrial myxoma, carotid artery disease, **APOE4** allele, polycythaemia, sickle cell anaemia, coagulopathies.

Risk factor **EMI** trap: vascular dementia's most important independent risk factors are specifically **SMALL** **VESSEL** **DISEASE** and **TYPE** 2 **DIABETES** — more important than age itself in this condition, in contrast to Alzheimer's disease where age and ApoE4 are the paired answers expected.

blocks.text: **CADASIL**: autosomal dominant with high penetrance, gene on the long arm of chromosome 19; presents with recurrent stroke around age 40-50 and often a migraine history; many later develop subcortical dementia and pseudobulbar palsy; **MRI** shows widespread white matter changes.

Imaging in vascular dementia: **CT** shows an increased number of infarcts; **MRI** white matter lesions are more numerous/severe than in **AD**; **SPECT** shows irregular perfusion deficits; **PET** shows reduced/uncoupled cerebral blood flow and metabolism; **MRS** shows absence of the phospholipid changes seen in **AD**.

Clonus and other pyramidal/asymmetric signs point to vascular rather than degenerative dementia in a mixed-presentation vignette — the exam expects recognition of focal neurological signs as the vascular discriminator even when cognitive symptoms look similar to **AD**.

bullets.text: **NINCDS-AIREN**: cerebrovascular disease on exam/imaging **PLUS** dementia within 3 months of stroke, **OR** abrupt/stepwise-fluctuating deterioration.

Three subtypes: single-stroke deficits (midbrain/thalamic, may fix or recover), multi-infarct (stepwise, minor episodes + stable periods), Binswanger's/small-vessel (subcortical, slow decline, gait/dysarthria, lacunae/leukoaraiosis on **MRI**).
**CADASIL**: autosomal dominant, chromosome 19; recurrent stroke age 40–50 with migraine history, later subcortical dementia/pseudobulbar palsy; widespread white-matter change on **MRI**.
Imaging: **MRI** white-matter lesions more numerous/severe than **AD**; **MRS** lacks the phospholipid changes seen in **AD**.

Risk factors: old age, hypertension (50% positive history), IHD, smoking, alcohol, hyperlipidaemia, atrial fibrillation, family history, valvular disease, atrial myxoma, carotid artery disease, **APOE4**, polycythaemia, sickle cell anaemia, coagulopathies.
Imaging: **CT** shows an increased number of infarcts; **SPECT** shows irregular perfusion deficits; **PET** shows reduced/uncoupled cerebral blood flow and metabolism.

blocks.text: **DLB** accounts for 15-==20%== of dementia cases. Lewy bodies (eosinophilic intracytoplasmic inclusions of abnormally phosphorylated neurofilament proteins aggregated with ubiquitin and alpha-synuclein) are found in brainstem, subcortical nuclei, limbic and neocortex.
Consensus criteria require progressive cognitive decline sufficient to interfere with function, plus core features (2 needed for probable, 1 for possible) and/or supportive features.

blocks.title: DLB Consensus Criteria — Core vs Supportive Features
rows: Core (2 needed for probable, 1 for possible)
Fluctuating cognition/attention; recurrent well-formed visual hallucinations; spontaneous parkinsonism (seen in ==70%==)
Repeated falls; syncope; transient loss of consciousness; neuroleptic sensitivity; systematised delusions; hallucinations in other modalities

blocks.forTopic: Consensus core features for probable Dementia with Lewy Bodies
expansion: Fluctuating cognition with marked variation in attention/alertness
Visual hallucinations — recurrent, well-formed and detailed

blocks.text: Clinical: paranoid delusions ==65%==, auditory hallucinations ==20%== (McKeith 1996); visual hallucinations (typically well-formed, often people/animals) in 60-==80%== of cases. ==60%== of patients are extremely sensitive to antipsychotics, and ~==50%== experience life-threatening adverse effects (McKeith 1992), which may be dose-related. Parkinsonism worsens at ~==10%==/year; ApoE ε4 frequency is increased; short-term memory and medial temporal lobes are relatively spared on imaging (**CT**/**MRI**/**SPECT-HMPAO**) compared with **AD**.

Pathologically, Lewy bodies are essential for confirmed diagnosis; associated (not essential) features include Lewy-related neuritis, plaques, neurofibrillary tangles, neuronal loss (especially locus coeruleus, substantia nigra, nucleus basalis of Meynert), synapse loss and spongiform change.

**Rivastigmine** showed significant improvement in delusions/hallucinations vs placebo in a large multicentre double-blind trial (McKeith et al 2000), but cholinesterase inhibitors are not currently licensed in the **UK** for **DLB** and a Cochrane review has questioned their benefit.

bullets.text: Consensus criteria: 2 of 3 core features (fluctuating cognition, recurrent well-formed visual hallucinations, spontaneous parkinsonism) = probable; 1 = possible.
Lewy bodies are essential for confirmed diagnosis; plaques/tangles/neuronal loss (locus coeruleus, substantia nigra, nucleus basalis) are associated but not essential.
**Rivastigmine** improved delusions/hallucinations vs placebo (McKeith 2000), but is not **UK**-licensed for **DLB** and a Cochrane review questioned its benefit.

blocks.text: **PD** is a prototype subcortical degenerative disease (substantia nigra, caudate, putamen, globus pallidus), impinging on the 3 M's — movement, mood, mentation. Bradyphrenia (slowed thinking) is common; cognitive symptom likelihood is greater with late-onset disease (>70y); ==10%==/year develop dementia, and ==78%== became demented over an 8-year follow-up (Aarsland & colleagues).

People with early **LBD**/**PD** dementia generally have **less severe** visual and verbal memory deficits but **more marked executive dysfunction** (planning, reasoning, sequencing) than people with **AD**; apraxia, dysphasia, alexia, agraphia, anomia and acalculia are also less pronounced than in **AD**. Even **non-demented** **PD** patients show neuropsychological impairment, mainly in visuospatial tasks and shifting cognitive sets, as measured by the **Wisconsin Card Sorting Test** or the **Stroop Test**. **PD** dementia impairs quality of life, worsens carer distress, increases the likelihood of residential care and **doubles mortality** (Burn & McKeith 2003).

Most patients treated with **levodopa** or dopamine agonists (e.g. apomorphine, **ropinirole**) develop neuropsychiatric side effects — visual hallucinations are the most common, alongside psychosis, anxiety, euphoria, mania, impulsive behaviour and delirium. Visual hallucinations with preserved insight are very common; persecutory delusions may occur.

Management of psychosis/hallucinations: first reduce **levodopa**/dopamine agonist dose; if ineffective, an atypical antipsychotic is used — **clozapine** is most successful, though **quetiapine** is reasonable to try first (lower success rate). Risk factors for psychosis in **PD**: older age, longer illness duration, cognitive impairment/dementia, illness severity, sleep deprivation, dopamine agonist use, polypharmacy.

Distinguishing **LBD** from **PD** dementia (McKeith et al 1996 international workshop): if motor and cognitive symptoms both develop within 12 months, diagnose **LBD**; if parkinsonism preceded dementia by >12 months, diagnose **PD** dementia. **SPECT** shows greater caudate involvement in **LBD**; **DAT** scan (123I-**FP-CIT**) detects the dopamine transporter deficiency common to **PD**/**LBD** and helps differentiate both from **AD**. **Rivastigmine** is licensed for **PD** dementia.

**LBD** vs **PD** dementia timing rule is tested repeatedly across both **SBA** and **EMI** formats: motor + cognitive symptoms both within 12 months = **LBD**; parkinsonism present >12 months **BEFORE** dementia onset = Parkinson's disease dementia — the 12-month cut-off itself (not just the general concept) is what's examined.

bullets.text: **PD** impinges on the 3 M's — movement, mood, mentation (cognition). Bradyphrenia (slowed thinking) is common; cognitive symptom likelihood is greater with late-onset disease (>70y).
**Levodopa**/dopamine agonists commonly cause visual hallucinations (most common), plus psychosis, anxiety, euphoria, mania, impulsivity, delirium; hallucinations with preserved insight are typical.

Management of **PD** psychosis: reduce **levodopa**/agonist dose first; if ineffective, atypical antipsychotic — **clozapine** most successful, **quetiapine** reasonable first try (lower success rate).

**LBD** vs **PD** dementia (McKeith 1996): motor + cognitive symptoms both within 12 months = **LBD**; parkinsonism preceding dementia by >12 months = **PD** dementia. **DAT**-scan detects the shared dopamine-transporter deficit vs **AD**; **rivastigmine** is licensed for **PD** dementia.

blocks.text: **FTD** encompasses Pick's disease (behavioural/frontal variant — the most common form), primary progressive aphasia, semantic dementia and corticobasal degeneration. Onset ranges 40-75y, accounting for ~==20%== of presenile dementia; some cases show chromosome 17 linkage. Early features are personality/behaviour change (disinhibition, apathy, mutism, repetitive behaviours); memory is affected later/less severely than in **AD** and spatial orientation is preserved; insight is lost early. Up to ==10%== of motor neuron disease patients show dementia features, with an aggressive course. SSRIs have limited benefit for behavioural symptoms; cholinesterase inhibitors are unlikely to help.

Pick's disease: onset usually 45-65y, men affected more than women, average illness duration 8 years, positive family history in ==50%==; autosomal dominant tau gene mutation (chromosome 17q21-22) with complete penetrance. Pick cells (swollen, pink on H&E) are pathognomonic; senile plaques/neurofibrillary tangles are absent. **CT**/**MRI** shows mild generalised but marked frontotemporal atrophy sparing the posterior third of the superior temporal gyrus — 'knife-blade atrophy'.

Primary progressive aphasia: non-fluent, effortful speech with relative sparing of other cognition, progressing to mutism; **MRI** shows perisylvian atrophy. Semantic dementia: fluent speech with impaired word meaning/naming; **MRI** shows disproportionate temporal atrophy (left > right, anterior > posterior).

bullets.text: **FTD** early features are personality/behaviour change (disinhibition, apathy, mutism, repetitive behaviours); memory affected later/less than **AD**, spatial orientation preserved, insight lost early.

Primary progressive aphasia: non-fluent speech, perisylvian atrophy. Semantic dementia: fluent speech, impaired word meaning, disproportionate (left>right, anterior>posterior) temporal atrophy.

blocks.text: Most dementia before age 65 is of the Alzheimer's type; other causes include vascular dementia, **FTD**, head injury and alcohol intoxication/metabolic disorders. Three dominant genes cause familial early-onset **AD**: **APP**, **PSEN1** and **PSEN2**. Language problems and visuospatial dysfunction are common in early-onset **AD**.

Progressive supranuclear palsy: onset in the sixth decade (range 45-75); presents with balance difficulty, abrupt falls/unsteady gait (retropulsion often the earliest complaint), slurred speech, dysphagia and personality change (sometimes agitated-depression-like apprehensiveness). The full syndrome (supranuclear ophthalmoplegia, pseudobulbar palsy, axial dystonia) may take a year or more to develop; vertical gaze palsy, loss of Bell's phenomenon and convergence, and a wide-eyed 'perpetual surprise' stare (lid retraction) are characteristic. Subcortical dementia is typical.

blocks.text: Onset is rapid with fluctuating severity over minutes/hours; features include clouded consciousness, reduced attention, disorientation, impaired recent memory/abstract thinking, sleep-wake disturbance with nocturnal worsening, and characteristically visual perceptual disturbances/hallucinations. Liposwski (1983) found no detectable cause in 5-==20%== of cases. Hyperactive delirium features increased motor activity/agitation; hypoactive delirium features reduced activity/lethargy and has a poorer prognosis.

"What % of delirium goes on to dementia?" — the correct answer (==5%==) is Liposwski's figure for cases with **NO** detectable cause, not a conversion-to-dementia rate; don't confuse it with the 10-==40%== who develop delirium during a hospital stay.

blocks.text: Prevalence: 10-==15%== of elderly patients have delirium on admission, with a further 10-==40%== developing it during their stay. Point prevalence: general population ==0.4%==; general hospital admissions 9-==30%==; post-operative 5-==75%==; **ICU** 12-==50%==; nursing homes up to ==60%==.

The major pathway is the dorsal tegmental pathway (mesencephalic reticular formation to tectum/thalamus); acetylcholine is the major implicated neurotransmitter. **EEG** characteristically shows generalised slowing, useful for differentiating delirium from depression/psychosis.

Rating scales: **DRS** (Delirium Rating Scale, most widely used, distinguishes delirium from dementia); **MMSE** (useful for monitoring cognitive change at follow-up, but weighted to left-hemisphere/dominant functions while delirium's core deficits, e.g. attention, relate more to non-dominant regions); **CTD** (Cognitive Test for Delirium, suitable when verbal interaction is compromised); **CAM** (Confusion Assessment Method, high sensitivity/specificity, but reduced sensitivity when used by nursing staff vs physicians).

Management: identify/treat the cause; environmental/supportive measures (education, reorientation, lighting, reduce noise, consistent staffing); avoid sedation unless severely agitated; correct sensory impairments; optimise hydration/nutrition/elimination/pain; safe environment. **NICE** advises short-term (<1 week) **haloperidol** or **olanzapine** if conservative measures fail; benzodiazepines may worsen agitation and increase falls/disinhibition in the elderly, but are useful specifically for alcohol/sedative withdrawal delirium.

Delirium in palliative care: the false statement to reject is "it always responds well to neuroleptics" — antipsychotics may reduce severity/duration **OR** further cloud the mental state; the exam wants you to know the response is not guaranteed.

bullets.text: Rapid onset, fluctuating severity; visual perceptual disturbances/hallucinations are characteristic. Hyperactive delirium = agitation; hypoactive = lethargy, worse prognosis.

Major pathway is dorsal tegmental (mesencephalic reticular formation → tectum/thalamus); acetylcholine is the key implicated neurotransmitter; **EEG** shows generalised slowing (helps differentiate from depression/psychosis).
**DRS** is the most widely used scale to distinguish delirium from dementia; **CAM** has high sensitivity/specificity but is less sensitive when used by nursing staff vs physicians.

Management: treat cause, environmental/supportive measures, avoid sedation unless severely agitated. **NICE**: short-term (<1wk) **haloperidol**/**olanzapine** if conservative measures fail; benzodiazepines can worsen agitation/falls but are specifically useful for alcohol/sedative withdrawal delirium.

blocks.text: Prevalence of clinically significant depression over 65 is 10-==15%==; overall major depression prevalence ~2-==3%== (higher in hospital/residential populations, Fountaulakis et al 2003): community 0.5-==1.5%==, clinical outpatients 5-==10%==, inpatients 10-==15%==, residential/nursing homes 15-==30%==. The '3 C's' — cardiovascular disease, **CNS** disorders (stroke, dementia, **PD**) and cancer — carry high depression risk; ==25%== of people with dementia develop depressive illness.

Late-life depression often shows less prominent low mood (Gurland 1976), more hypochondriasis/somatic concern, poor subjective memory (dementia-like picture), late-onset neurotic symptoms (marked anxiety/**OCD**/hysterical features), and apathy/poor motivation rather than classic sadness.

Compared with early-onset depression (depressive cognitions, severe psychomotor change in up to ==30%==, higher familial loading), later-onset depression shows cognitive impairment in ~==70%== of cases, more anxiety/neuroticism, less familial depression, and greater life stress/psychological vulnerability.

Risk factors for late-life depression: female sex, poor health, disability, poor perceived social support. Neuroimaging: ischaemic changes, reduced frontal/temporal grey matter, sulcal widening, reduced caudate and hippocampal volume, ventricular enlargement.

bullets.text: Late-life depression: less prominent low mood (Gurland 1976), more hypochondriasis/somatic concern, dementia-like subjective memory complaints, late-onset neurotic symptoms, apathy rather than classic sadness.

Early-onset depression: more depressive cognitions, up to ==30%== severe psychomotor change, higher familial loading. Later-onset: more cognitive impairment/anxiety, less familial loading, more life stress.

Risk factors: female sex, poor health, disability, poor perceived social support. Neuroimaging: ischaemic changes, reduced frontal/temporal grey matter, reduced caudate/hippocampal volume, ventricular enlargement.

blocks.text: Antidepressant response rate in older people is comparable to younger adults (**NNT** ~4, similar to other age groups, Chew-Graham et al 2004). Start at lower doses but titrate to standard treatment doses; **NICE** recommends **SSRI** first-line for late-onset depression given relative safety in overdose, though **GI** bleed risk is somewhat increased and all SSRIs can cause hyponatraemia. Response may take 6-8 weeks; ~==30%== do not respond to medication (Mottram et al 1998).

**ECT** is the most effective treatment for severe depression (~==80%== recovery), well tolerated even in very elderly patients (Tew et al 1999), and particularly effective in psychotic depression (Baldwin et al 2002). Post-**ECT** confusion/cognitive impairment is more likely in the elderly and needs monitoring; bilateral electrode placement worsens memory impairment more but may give a faster response.

Psychological interventions are rarely offered to older depressed patients despite being as effective as medication for mild-moderate episodes (McCusker 1998, Pinquart & Sorenson 2001). Combining antidepressants with psychotherapy is more effective than either alone, especially for relapse prevention (Reynolds 1999). **CBT** is best-established (Thompson 2001); **IPT** is effective for relapse prevention; problem-solving therapy has smaller evidence (Arean 1993); family therapy has been adapted for older adults (Benbow 1990).

At 2-year follow-up: ==33%== well, ==33%== still depressed, ==21%== dead (meta-analysis). Depression worsens medical outcomes — depressed elderly patients are almost four times more likely to die within 4 months of an **MI**, with raised platelet aggregation and elevated plasma interleukin-6 (linked to increased fracture risk via bone resorption).

Psychological therapies are as effective as medication for mild-moderate episodes but rarely offered; combining antidepressants + psychotherapy beats either alone, especially for relapse prevention. **CBT** best-established, **IPT** effective for relapse prevention.
Depressed elderly patients are ~4x more likely to die within 4 months of an **MI** (raised platelet aggregation, elevated **IL-6** linked to fracture risk via bone resorption).

blocks.text: Cognitive deficits occur more when depression first onsets in older age (Holroyd & Duryee 1997); late-onset depression shows attention/executive deficits (frontal), while recurrent early-onset depression shows episodic memory deficits (temporal) (Rapp et al 2005). Some elderly patients develop pseudodementia (dementia-like picture during a depressive episode that subsides with remission), mostly in late-onset major depression; ~==40%== of these go on to develop true dementia within 3 years (Alexopoulos 2005).

Pseudodementia vs dementia: precise-datable onset vs onset dateable only broadly; short vs long symptom duration before help-seeking; rapid vs slow progression; usual vs unusual prior psychiatric history; patients complain much/emphasise disability vs complain little/conceal disability; nocturnal accentuation uncommon vs common; attention/concentration well preserved vs faulty; 'don't know' answers vs near-miss answers; recent-and-remote memory loss vs recent-worse-than-remote memory loss.

blocks.text: Vascular depression (Alexopoulos): cerebral ischaemic damage to frontal-subcortical circuits may predispose/precipitate/perpetuate late-onset depression; clinical features include apathy, psychomotor retardation, poor executive function, less depressive thinking (less guilt/worthlessness) and late age of onset; verbal fluency and object naming are most impaired cognitively.

**MRI** deep white matter lesions (DWMLs) are more common in depressed than non-depressed older people, more common in late-onset than early-onset depression, and predict poorer antidepressant response (Simpson et al) — though patients with vascular depression may still recover with **ECT**, albeit with increased post-treatment delirium risk. Ischaemia-promoting antidepressants (dopamine/norepinephrine enhancing) may be favoured; ischaemia-inhibiting agents (adrenergic blockers) are best avoided (Alexopoulos 2005).

bullets.text: Late-onset depression shows attention/executive (frontal) deficits; recurrent early-onset depression shows episodic memory (temporal) deficits (Rapp 2005). Pseudodementia occurs mostly in late-onset major depression.
Vascular depression (Alexopoulos): apathy, psychomotor retardation, poor executive function, less guilt/worthlessness, late onset; verbal fluency/object naming most impaired.

**MRI** deep white-matter lesions are commoner in depression (esp. late-onset) and predict poorer antidepressant response, though **ECT** can still work (with higher post-treatment delirium risk); favour dopamine/norepinephrine-enhancing antidepressants, avoid adrenergic blockers.

blocks.text: Mania accounts for 5-==10%== of mood disorders in the elderly; 1-year prevalence of bipolar disorder ≥65 is ==0.4%== (vs ==1.4%== in younger adults). Average onset age 55, female:male ratio 2:1. Mania is often followed by a depressive episode and mixed presentations are more common than in younger patients; insight is almost always absent.

First-episode mania in late life has lower familial loading than younger-onset bipolar disorder and more often represents secondary mania (temporally linked to a physical illness/drug, usually without a family history) — causes include stroke (commonest, particularly right-sided lesions), head injury, tumours, endocrine disorders, **HIV** infection, and medication including steroids and antiparkinsonian drugs. Cognitive impairment is seen in a fifth to a third of elderly manic patients, and cerebral white matter lesions are more frequent in late-life mania.

**Lithium** is first-line prophylaxis but at lower dosages — a lower therapeutic range of ~0.4-0.6 mmol/L is suggested (Shulman 2002). **Valproate** is also popular; antipsychotics are added for more severe illness at age-appropriate doses.

bullets.text: First-episode late-life mania has lower familial loading and is often secondary (stroke commonest, especially right-sided; also head injury, tumours, endocrine, **HIV**, steroids/antiparkinsonian drugs); cognitive impairment in a fifth to a third of elderly manic patients.
**Lithium** first-line but at a lower therapeutic range (~0.4–0.6 mmol/L, Shulman 2002); **valproate** also popular; antipsychotics added for more severe illness at age-appropriate doses.

blocks.text: Kraepelin introduced 'paraphrenia' (1913); Kleist described 'Involutional Paranoia' around the same time. Current consensus divides late-onset psychosis into late-onset (after 40) and very-late-onset (after 60). Late paraphrenia represents ~==10%== of elderly psychiatric hospital inpatients; community prevalence is 0.1-==4%==, incidence 10-26 per 100,000/year; point prevalence of paranoid ideation in the general elderly population is 4-==6%== (most of these have dementia). Significantly more females are affected.

First-rank symptoms, negative symptoms and thought disorder are all uncommon in late paraphrenia. Partition delusions (people/gas/radiation passing through walls or ceilings) are characteristic. **ICD** provides no separate diagnostic category for paraphrenia — patients must be classified as delusional disorder or schizophrenia.

Late-onset schizophrenia (Palmer et al 2001) shows fewer negative symptoms, better antipsychotic response, better neuropsychological performance, more visual hallucinations, less formal thought disorder, less affective blunting, and a greater risk of tardive dyskinesia (5-6x greater than younger adults, Kane 1999). Relatives of very-late-onset patients have lower morbid risk for schizophrenia than relatives of early-onset patients (==7%== siblings, ==3%== parents of all probands).

Risk factors for late-onset psychosis: age-related frontal/temporal cortical changes, cognitive decline, social isolation, sensory deprivation (hearing/visual loss), polypharmacy, paranoid/schizoid personality traits, precipitating life events, female sex, and family history (weaker than younger-onset schizophrenia).

Treatment: exclude Lewy body dementia before starting antipsychotics; elderly patients are more prone to late-emerging (tardive) **EPSE**, and atypicals carry vascular risk concerns; follow 'start low and go slow'. **Clozapine**'s efficacy in treatment-resistant early-onset schizophrenia is well established but toxicity/monitoring burden limits its use in the elderly to treatment resistance and severe tardive dyskinesia.

items.text: Tardive dyskinesia risk with antipsychotics in the elderly is increased 5-6x compared with younger adults — a specific figure recurring in both dementia (**CSM** **olanzapine**/**risperidone**) and late-onset schizophrenia contexts.

sections.title: 19. Neurotic Disorders & Alcohol/Substance Misuse in Old Age

blocks.text: Neurotic disorder prevalence is 1-==10%== with female predominance. Anxiety disorders are the most prevalent psychiatric disorders excluding dementia, but prevalence decreases with age; phobic disorder is the most prevalent anxiety disorder (fear of falling is common), while panic disorder is the least common. Non-specific anxiety, hypochondriacal and depressive symptoms predominate; obsessional, phobic, dissociative and conversion disorders are less common. **Fluoxetine** (**GAD**, **PTSD**), **citalopram** (panic), **paroxetine** (**GAD**, **PTSD**) and **venlafaxine** (**GAD**) are **UK**-licensed for anxiety disorders in this context, with a warning of transient anxiety increase in the first 1-2 weeks. Most cases of agoraphobia developing after age 65 are **not** panic-induced, but arise following an alarming experience of physical ill health.

Older people encounter alcohol problems at lower intake levels than the general population owing to physical/cognitive ageing, pharmacokinetic change and comorbidity/medication interactions; the general-population 'safe-drinking' levels (**21 units/week for men, 14 for women**) may be inappropriately high for older people, and most guidelines recommend no more than one drink/day instead. Men are >2x as likely as women to exceed weekly safe-drinking limits, but women report more late-onset problems; widowed/divorced men are more likely to drink heavily, while among women it is those who are married who have the highest consumption.

blocks.title: Early-onset vs Late-onset Alcohol Problems in Old Age

blocks.text: **Chlordiazepoxide** can be used to treat withdrawal symptoms. Late-onset alcohol problems are more receptive to treatment and more likely to remit spontaneously than early-onset problems. **Disulfiram** should generally be avoided in the elderly (risk of acute confusional state) and is contraindicated with hypertension, cardiac failure, stroke or ischaemic heart disease; **acamprosate** and **naltrexone** are the other relapse-prevention options, and **thiamine** should be given to prevent Wernicke-Korsakoff syndrome.

Illicit drug use is far less common than alcohol/medication misuse in older people (**ECA** lifetime prevalence ==1.6%==). Benzodiazepines are the most commonly prescribed psychotropic in this age group (==17%== of community-dwelling older people in one Irish study) and carry higher risk of falls, confusional states and amnesia.

bullets.text: Anxiety prevalence decreases with age but remains commonest psychiatric disorder (excl. dementia); phobic disorder most prevalent, panic least. **Fluoxetine**/**paroxetine** (**GAD**/**PTSD**), **citalopram** (panic), **venlafaxine** (**GAD**) are **UK**-licensed — watch for transient anxiety increase in the first 1–2 weeks.

Older people develop alcohol problems at lower intake levels; men >2x more likely to exceed weekly limits, but women report more late-onset problems; widowed/divorced men drink most heavily, married women drink most among women.

**Disulfiram** generally avoided in the elderly (confusional state risk; contraindicated with hypertension/cardiac failure/stroke/**IHD**); **acamprosate**/**naltrexone** are alternatives; give **thiamine** to prevent Wernicke-Korsakoff.

sections.title: 20. Suicide & Deliberate Self-Harm in Old Age

blocks.text: Deliberate self-harm incidence is highest in the young and declines with age, while completed suicide rises with age; suicidal intent behind **DSH** is significantly greater in older people, so **DSH** over 75 should be regarded clinically as failed suicide. **DSH** raw female:male ratio is ~3:2 but the proportionate ratio is ~1:1 (fewer men survive to old age); completed suicide is male-predominant.

Drug overdose is the commonest **DSH** method (benzodiazepines, analgesics, antidepressants most frequent); self-cutting is next most common. About half of older **DSH** patients have major depressive disorder, up to a third have alcohol abuse, and under ==10%== have no psychiatric diagnosis at all; alcohol abuse plus depression compounds **DSH** risk. Risk factors: physical illness, widowhood/divorce/separation, social isolation/loneliness, living alone, unresolved grief.

In completed suicide, men outnumber women 3-4:1; associated with divorce, widowhood and single status (widowers more than widows). **UK** methods: drug overdose (especially women, often analgesics), hanging (especially men), suffocation, jumping. Careful planning is typical, and about half leave a note. A prior **DSH** history is found in ~1/3 of older suicide victims; ==70%== have major depressive disorder at time of death, and untreated/undertreated depression and comorbid physical illness are risk factors.

Social risk factors: isolation, lack of a confidant, concern over dependents, a move to residential care. Bereavement itself is not an extra risk factor unless grief is prolonged beyond a year. Personality correlates: higher Neuroticism and lower Openness to Experience (Duberstein et al 1994); anankastic (obsessional) and anxious traits (Harwood et al 2001).

bullets.text: **DSH** incidence falls with age while completed suicide rises; **DSH** over 75 should be treated clinically as failed suicide given the higher suicidal intent behind it.
Drug overdose is the commonest **DSH** method; about half of older **DSH** patients have **MDD**, up to a third alcohol abuse, and <==10%== no psychiatric diagnosis at all.

Social risk factors: isolation, lack of a confidant, concern over dependents, move to residential care. Bereavement alone isn't an added risk unless grief is prolonged beyond a year. Personality correlates: high Neuroticism, low Openness, anankastic/anxious traits.

sections.title: 21. Personality Disorders in Old Age & Diogenes Syndrome

blocks.text: Overall prevalence of personality disorder in older people is 5-==10%==; cautiousness, obsessionality and introversion tend to increase with age (Howard & Bergmann 1993). Abrams et al's (1999) meta-analytic review of 30 studies found little difference in **PD** prevalence/cluster distribution between <50 and >50 age groups, though a British community study (Cohen 1994) found older subjects significantly less likely to have any **PD** (==6.6%== vs ==10.5%==, **OR** 0.42), almost entirely due to a threefold higher Cluster B prevalence (especially antisocial and histrionic) in younger cohorts — the highest single elderly **PD** prevalence was obsessive-compulsive **PD** at ==3.3%==. Diagnostic criteria are age-biased, requiring evidence of dysfunction from younger ages that may not be available. Psychopathy is said to burn out with advancing age, and criminal behaviour is rare in the elderly (~1% of male offenders are >60 years).

Association with other diagnoses: **PD** patients are four times more likely to have persistent/relapsing depression (Morse & Lynch 2004); **GAD** and substance use disorders are also more common with **PD**. Avoidant, dependent and compulsive traits occur particularly with depressive illness; hypochondriacal **PD** is associated with psychotic depression; paranoid personality traits may predate late paraphrenia in patients who have never married/lived alone for years.

Personality change occurs in organic disorders (Burns 1992); two-thirds of people with dementia show negative personality change, in one of four patterns: alteration at dementia onset with little subsequent change; ongoing change with disease progression; regression to previously disturbed behaviours; or no change at all.

Diogenes syndrome ('senile squalor syndrome'): eccentric, reclusive self-neglect with filthy living conditions, often with hoarding of valueless possessions (syllogomania); patients are typically oblivious to their condition and resistant to help, making a therapeutic alliance and management notoriously difficult.

Hoarding differential in the elderly: Diogenes syndrome (personality-disorder-driven self-neglect), **OCD**-driven hoarding (anxiety-associated), and Pick's disease (hoarding as one of a range of stereotyped/repetitive behaviours) are three distinct causes tested in the same **EMI** — match the accompanying features (self-neglect vs anxiety vs other frontal behavioural stereotypies), not just "hoarding" alone.

Two-thirds of people with dementia show negative personality change, in one of four patterns: onset change only, ongoing change with progression, regression to old disturbed behaviours, or no change.
Diogenes syndrome: eccentric, reclusive self-neglect, filthy living conditions, hoarding of valueless items (syllogomania); patients are oblivious and resistant to help.

blocks.text: Insomnia is the commonest sleep disorder in old age; symptoms must persist >2 weeks with impaired functioning before intervention. Treatment (**NICE** **CKS**): treat underlying cause; sleep hygiene advice; short-acting benzodiazepines/Z-drugs (**GABA**-mediated) or **melatonin** agonists (only if >55y with symptoms >4 weeks); refer to **IAPT**/**CBT** (stimulus control, sleep restriction, relaxation therapy) if symptoms persist beyond 2 weeks; hypnotic use should be restricted to those meeting diagnostic criteria and limited to ≤2 weeks.

Circadian rhythm disorders are common in nursing homes (inadequate light exposure, suprachiasmatic nucleus degeneration); advanced sleep phase syndrome is probably the commonest, treated with bright light therapy, evening **melatonin** and chronotherapy. Sleep-related breathing disorders (apnoea/hypopnoea) need a bed-partner history and polysomnography; treatment includes weight reduction, **CPAP** and oral appliances/**UPPP**.

**REM** sleep behaviour disorder (loss of **REM** muscle atonia, enacted dream activity) is much more prevalent in Parkinson's disease (15-==34%==), multiple system atrophy (==90%==) and **LBD** than the general population (0.5-==0.8%==), and can predate a dementia diagnosis by years to decades; treatment includes a safe sleeping environment, **clonazepam**, **melatonin** or **pramipexole**.

blocks.text: Age-related oestrogen decline causes vaginal dryness/atrophy and dyspareunia in women; testosterone decline after the fifth decade reduces desire in men; impotence affects 10-==20%== of men ≥70. Despite these physiological changes, sexual satisfaction does not necessarily decline with age, though sexual history is rarely covered in clinical assessment despite being a recommended part of it.

Medical causes of sexual dysfunction include Parkinson's disease, stroke, arthritis and incontinence. Drugs causing erectile dysfunction include alcohol, benzodiazepines, antidepressants (**trazodone** — priapism), beta-blockers, and antihypertensives such as thiazide diuretics and spironolactone. Physical illness can cause anxiety about the safety of sex (post-**MI**/**CVA**) or undermine confidence (post-mastectomy/colostomy).

Inappropriate sexual behaviour in dementia is uncommon overall (~==7%== in Alzheimer's, higher at ~==18%== in care homes), may reflect frontal lobe pathology, and can be assessed/managed using the **ABC** (antecedents, behaviour, consequences) framework. Capacity to consent to sexual activity in dementia is decision-specific and can be a particular concern around new relationships.

bullets.text: Sexual satisfaction doesn't necessarily decline with age despite oestrogen/testosterone decline, though sexual history is rarely taken despite being recommended.

Drugs causing **ED** include alcohol, benzodiazepines, antidepressants (**trazodone** → priapism), beta-blockers, thiazides/spironolactone; physical illness can undermine sexual confidence/safety concerns post-**MI**/**CVA**/mastectomy/colostomy.
Inappropriate sexual behaviour in dementia may reflect frontal pathology, managed with the **ABC** framework; capacity to consent to sexual activity is decision-specific.

blocks.text: Older adults should have access to the full range of psychological treatments though access is often harder in practice; **CBT** is the most commonly used, including for dementia caregivers. Cognitive impairment may limit engagement; transference issues may be altered since the therapist is often younger than the patient; dependency, loss of sexuality and death are important themes.

A third of people who lose a spouse meet criteria for major depression in the first month, and half of these remain depressed at 1 year; treatment should start earlier with suicidal ideation, severe functional impairment, prior depression history, or other severe-depression signs. In the elderly, 10-==20%== of surviving spouses develop depression requiring treatment in the first year.

Elderly people are less likely to become depressed than younger adults in the first months of widowhood, but rates of major depression become similar across ages by the end of the second year, by which point ==14%== of bereaved elderly have major depression (vs 1-==4%== of the elderly population generally, Alexopoulos 2005).

Normal grief has four phases: shock/protest (numbness, disbelief, acute dysphoria); preoccupation (yearning, searching, anger); disorganisation (despair, acceptance); resolution — with substantial improvement expected within 2-6 months.
